name: South Carolina
summary_text: A trans visitor to South Carolina enters under the United States federal document and screening regime before state law applies. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, issuing new passports only as M or F, while previously issued X-marker passports remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.  Entry screening adds exposure. The State Department announced on 25 February 2025 that it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flags visa applicants with an internal marking, and treats a declared gender other than the one assigned at birth as fraud carrying a permanent bar. Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures can involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that risk outing a trans traveller.  Facilities are the sharpest South Carolina-specific exposure. Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 into law on 15 May 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth. The Senate amended the bill before passage, and the ACLU of South Carolina issued a response on 18 May 2026 framing it as discrimination against trans students in both K-12 and higher education.  The measure extends a pre-existing restriction on school restrooms into campus settings. A July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment, which ranks states on the severity of adult and youth law by reading bills, places South Carolina among the escalating states rather than in the harshest tier.  Custody carries a further state-layer restriction: South Carolina operates a "freeze-frame" policy limiting the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated. Federal custody is separately affected by the Bureau of Prisons adoption of Florida-based policies for transgender inmates from 2026, which mandate short haircuts, withdrawal of hormone medication and substitution of psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs, and by the Bureau's cessation of reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025.

name: South Dakota
summary_text:
South Dakota stands under the national framework of the United States, and that federal layer carries the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad.
 State law now restricts facility use as well. Governor Larry Rhoden's office announced on Friday 21 March 2025 that he had signed House Bill 1259 the previous day, barring trans people from restrooms matching their gender identity in public schools and state-owned buildings. The measure took effect on 1 July 2025 and marks the first time a restriction of this kind has been placed on the books in South Dakota; comparable legislation failed in 2016, in 2017, twice in 2018 and in 2022.
 House Bill 1259 passed the South Dakota House of Representatives by a 49-21 vote and limits restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas in state-run facilities to the same 'biological sex.' Its institutional scope reaches K-12 schools and state colleges, including off-campus activities, as well as prisons and other state facilities. The bill's 'reasonable accommodation' clause and the floor debate over it raised the prospect that incarcerated trans people would be placed in solitary confinement in order to comply with the law.
 South Dakota is listed among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults in Erin Reed's July 2026 anti-trans legal-risk assessment for transgender travellers, compiled from five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric identifying the most damaging bills. Federal policies continue to create legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide.
